PLURALISM AND MORALITY; FUNDAMENTALISM AND RELATIVISM - CHAPTER OVERVIEW
- Opening image: Bloody Sunday, 1972, when thirteen people were shot dead by British soldiers during an anti-internment rally in Derry city. Question: "Whose truth is it anyway?"
- The chapter covers: pluralism; tolerance; fallacies in arguments; bioethics (case study: stem-cell research on human embryos); social ethics (case study: marriage of homosexuals); other contentious issues; the two extremes of fundamentalism and relativism.

PLURALISM
- Even classmates find it hard to agree (the desert island exercise from the last chapter). It is much harder for a whole society.
- The Christian moral vision is one way of understanding humanity and giving a framework for living, but not everyone shares it.
- Most Western societies are now pluralist: they include more than one way of viewing the world - a plurality of visions about humanity.
- Pluralism: there are many different schools of thought within society. All groups have a right to carry out their cultural and religious practices.
- Question: which views should be reflected in the law of the State or in promoting the common good? This leads to moral conflict between groups with different moral convictions - an inevitable pattern in a modern democratic society.
- A healthy society listens with respect to all points of view, but eventually must order itself around some set of common moral principles. There must be a general consensus, in civil law, about the society's priorities and values.
- The challenge: how to arrive at a sense of the common good while also respecting civil rights.

TOLERANCE
- Tolerance: a frame of mind that accepts others' right to hold and express a viewpoint we disagree with.
- It is an important virtue in a pluralist society, and important for religious and civil liberties.
- But tolerance is not the final answer to all problems; a society must choose to live by some common values.
- One cannot tolerate what one believes to be destructive. Example: you might tolerate loud noise from a party on a Friday night, but not someone bullying a person who cannot defend themselves.
- Photo example: Lesbian, Gay and Bisexual Rights launch at USI (Union of Students in Ireland) headquarters, urging a culture of tolerance to stop discrimination and intimidation.

FALLACIES IN ARGUMENTS
- When one holds a deep conviction it is appropriate to argue against the reasoning of an opposing group and to protest. But people commonly make mistakes (fallacies) in argument.
- Argumentum ad hominem (spelled 'ad hominum' in the book): attacking the personality of the opponent instead of the content of the issue. Very common but a faulty basis for argument. Example: "How could you lecture me about morals: you don't even dress yourself decently!"
- Emotions and loyalties: people see the same incident from different perspectives. Example: "It should have been a penalty, but the away team will never get a penalty at Old Trafford. Ever!"
- Emotive language: language that has little to do with the actual issue; playing on fears, prejudices and stereotypes, or using anecdotes to make general points. Example: claiming all refugees and asylum-seekers are "spongers" and a threat, pointing to trouble a group caused in Dublin.

BIOETHICS
- Bioethics: the study of ethical issues that arise in the world of medicine. It can be very emotive because it involves health and life and death.
- Everyday medical dilemmas: whether to continue an expensive treatment that may cause more stress than healing; whether to put an A&E unit in a local hospital or a central location with more backup; which patients go on a transplant waiting list and why.
- Public debate focuses on abortion (a reality in many Western European countries), possible reproductive cloning of humans, and euthanasia (allowed in a few jurisdictions).
- With medical advances these discussions keep changing, so bioethics must also change and adapt.

CASE STUDY: STEM-CELL RESEARCH USING THE HUMAN EMBRYO
- The issue: should scientists be allowed to carry out research on human embryos to learn more about the human body?
- Source: a submission to the British House of Lords Select Committee on stem-cell research.
- Stem cells: versatile cells that can reproduce themselves and produce more specialised cells; of great potential value in repairing and regenerating damaged cells and tissue.
- Conditions potentially treatable: Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, heart disease, stroke and diabetes.
- Sources of stem cells: the early human embryo, the older embryo or foetus, the newborn baby (e.g. umbilical cord), the older child and the adult. As a person develops, stem cells become more committed to a particular destination in the body, though some flexibility remains.
- Embryonic stem cells can come from an embryo or foetus during or after an abortion or after a miscarriage, or from the early embryo after in vitro fertilisation (IVF). The IVF embryo may be 'spare' (surplus to the infertile couple's needs) or specifically created for experiments.
- UK legislation allows such use of foetal tissue up to fourteen days old. The procedure has not yet been widely used to great benefit; much research remains.

ARGUMENTS IN FAVOUR OF EMBRYO STEM-CELL RESEARCH
- Experimentation has always been an accepted part of medical research.
- It will probably lead to great advances in treating serious diseases such as cancer.
- No person is being harmed.
- The goal is greater health; it is a moral duty to do one's utmost to protect health and life, including research.
- A vaccine for polio was discovered using discarded foetuses from abortions.
- IVF embryos will be discarded anyway, so with the parents' consent they should be used for a good purpose.
- Moral principle: the greater good of humanity is served by the results and insights of this research.
- Underlying ethical positions: the embryo is not a life but a potential life; more embryos than necessary are produced in IVF, so they might as well be used; the possible outcome outweighs the arguments against; consequences must always be considered and might make an otherwise wrong act right in certain cases.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST EMBRYO STEM-CELL RESEARCH
- The embryo is a human life. No human life should be used as a means to an end. Its rights include the right not to be attacked, used or commercialised, and the right to care from its genetic parents. It is irresponsible to let one's genetic material create an embryo with no chance of implantation. IVF for research and cloning for research are wrong for similar reasons.
- Human experimentation requires consent; an embryo cannot give consent.
- The Helsinki Declaration on Medical Research Involving Human Subjects condemns research that is without the subject's consent, harmful to the subject, or puts the interests of science and society above the subject's interests.
- In genuine doubt about the humanity of the subject, err on the side of caution; embryos should be protected by law.
- Moral principle: a human person should not be used for experimentation without consent; it is an abuse of the person.
- Underlying ethical positions: an embryo is a human life, not just a potential life; the end, however good, does not justify the means; some acts are objectively wrong whatever the consequences.

CAUSES OF CONFLICT (STEM CELLS)
- Two elements: how people view the status of the embryo; whether people believe the results of an action make it morally right.
- People within the same religious community may take different positions.
- The Catholic Church opposes stem-cell research on embryos because an embryo is a human life and cannot be experimented on, however laudable the outcome.
- John Paul II (2003): "The Church respects and supports scientific research when it has a genuinely human orientation, avoiding any form of instrumentalisation or destruction of the human being and keeping itself free from the slavery of political and economic interests."
- Pontifical Academy for Life (2003): the human embryo "deserves the full respect that is due to every human person"; embryos cannot consent; any experimentation on the embryo that does not aim at direct benefits for its own health "cannot be considered morally licit".

SOCIAL ETHICS
- Social policy issues cause conflict among people with different ethical beliefs. In recent Irish debate these included human sexuality in the public arena: availability of contraception, rights of homosexuals, support of marriage and the family, availability of divorce.
- Case study: the right of homosexual people to marry in the State (as debated when the book was written).

ARGUMENTS IN FAVOUR OF RECOGNISING MARRIAGE OF HOMOSEXUALS
- Every person has a right to marry, whatever their sexual orientation.
- To deprive gay people of that right is discrimination.
- Marriage brings stability to gay relationships and easier access to civil rights, e.g. inheritance rights.
- It makes society more aware of the equality of gay people.
- Moral principle: equality of opportunity for every person.
- Underlying ethical position: homosexuality is a reality in the nature of human persons and should be fully accepted as such.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST MARRIAGE OF HOMOSEXUALS
- Marriage is the bonding of a man and a woman, so homosexual people cannot partake of marriage.
- It is against the code of belief of many religions.
- Denying it is not discrimination but adherence to belief in marriage as a union of man and woman open to new life.
- Moral principle: marriage is of its essence a lifelong bonding of a man and a woman, with the support of family and children.
- Underlying ethical position: homosexual acts are against the moral law and the natural law.

CAUSES OF CONFLICT (MARRIAGE)
- The causes are multilayered.
- Supporters: the issue is respect for difference and human rights regardless of sexual orientation; some within church communities also support the right to marry.
- Many opponents say their stance comes not from discrimination or homophobia (fear of homosexuality) but from their concept of marriage and family.
- People of faith argue in both directions from religious belief and scripture.
- The Catholic Church rejects marriage between homosexuals as incompatible with its understanding of marriage. CCC 2360: "Sexuality is ordered to the conjugal love of man and woman. In marriage the physical intimacy of the spouses becomes a sign and pledge of spiritual communion. Marriage bonds between baptised persons are sanctified by the sacrament."
- Compendium of the Social Doctrine of the Church (2004): the family is "born of the intimate communion of life and love founded on the marriage between one man and one woman"; it is "the first and vital cell of society" and "a divine institution".

RANGE OF ETHICAL DISCUSSION
- Other contentious issues about how the common good is expressed in civil law:
- Neutrality: stay outside military alliances or take part in common defence?
- Media ethics and libel laws: more controls to protect people's good name, or would that limit free expression and investigative journalism?
- Balancing environmental and economic issues, e.g. waste disposal and community safety.
- Is there a right to total freedom of expression, even including racist comments?
- How broad should policy be on accepting asylum-seekers fleeing persecution or seeking economic survival?
- A DNA database could identify rapists immediately, but would it impinge on privacy and freedom?
- Almost every public debate has a moral dimension. Division often comes from a principle passionately held (e.g. the embryo is a human being) or from how a person reaches a moral decision (e.g. the end sometimes justifies the means).

THE TWO EXTREMES
- Most modern debate is marked by two extremes: fundamentalism and relativism.
- A fundamentalist holds there is a truth that must be adhered to by all.
- A relativist says no one can impose truth on others; truth is always a matter for each individual to decide.

FUNDAMENTALISM: KEEPING THE TRUTH
- Fundamentalist: one who follows a truth literally; has a strict belief in the law as laid down and follows it without exception.
- Fundamentalism is a general term, not tied to any one movement or religion. It is more likely in traditions that stress correct belief, and where there has been a move away from seeing morality as a set of laws; fundamentalists react against what they see as relaxing moral laws.
- Many movements start as a reaction to an opposite extreme. Fundamentalism first appeared in Protestant American churches as a reaction to the liberal theology of the nineteenth century, from a desire to be clear about the fundamental, essential truths of the faith.
- The Scopes trial, Tennessee, 1925: John T. Scopes, a teacher, was taken to court for teaching the theory of evolution, against the Butler Law (a state law). Fundamentalists had made it illegal to teach contrary to their understanding of the Creation account in Genesis.
- Fundamentalists stressed the authority of scripture and right living. The movement grew through the last century in an era of increasing pluralism and uncertainty. It is closely aligned with conservative right-wing political movements. Recently US fundamentalist Christian groups have gained political clout and sought to influence laws on abortion and same-sex unions.
- Because of the more centralised structure of the Catholic Church, a fundamentalist movement did not surface in Catholicism to the same extent until after the Second Vatican Council. When it did, it was marked by literalism and dogmatism.
- Literalism: taking the literal meanings of words or texts.
- Dogmatism: asserting beliefs.
- At a glance, fundamentalism is: a desire to be true to basic objective truths; characterised by literal and dogmatic interpretations of scripture and moral laws.

ISLAMIC FUNDAMENTALISM
- Has religious, cultural and political characteristics.
- Aims to define clearly the most basic characteristics of Islam and to enshrine Islamic laws in countries where Islam is the main religion. It seeks to limit Western influence.
- It strengthened in North Africa and the Middle East in the last decades of the twentieth century.
- In its most extreme and radical form it gives rise to groups such as the Taliban in Afghanistan.
- Warning: do not fall into a stereotype of Islam, judging all Muslims by what is seen in the media.
- Case study - honour killings in Iraq: a seventeen-year-old, Akhmed, gave himself up at Jazaar police station in north Baghdad after shooting his mother (Senija), his half-brother (Ali) and his four-year-old sister (Jenan), because his mother had had an affair with Ali and neighbours in Saddam City (a poor Shiite district) were gossiping. He said it was his duty "to wash away the scandal and uphold my family's good name". After the fall of Saddam Hussein he could buy a Kalashnikov for $35.
- Honour killings: revenge murders to restore the reputation of a family shamed by scandal; most victims are young Iraqi women who rebelled against a strict moral code. They increased sharply amid the breakdown in security after the fall of Saddam Hussein.
- Under Iraqi law at the time honour killings were not considered a grave offence; he faced a maximum of one year in prison.
- Islam respects life as a gift from God; death can only come at a time allotted by God (Qur'an 3:145). The chapter invites comparison with Jesus and the woman caught in adultery (John 8:1-11).

RELATIVISM: WHOSE TRUTH IS IT ANYWAY?
- Relativism: the view that we can never agree on what is ultimately right and wrong. Different religious and cultural groups hold their own views, but these are subjective; there is no objective truth.
- Subjective view: the view, attitude or belief of the subject. Example: "I feel that Kerry is the best football team in the country."
- Objective view: a universal truth that applies everywhere. Example: "Based on the results of the championship of 2005, Tyrone are the champions."
- Moral relativism: there is no objective truth in ethics.
- Religions generally oppose relativism. Christian ethics disagrees because God has revealed a way of life and being. Through the natural law written in our nature, God's revelation in scripture, and Christ, all peoples can know the truth about good and evil. This is objective truth - true for everyone, not just believers.
- Beckwith and Koukl: relativism is "the view that when it comes to moral issues there are no universally objective right or wrong answers... and no reasonable or rational ways by which to make moral distinctions that apply in every time, in every place, and to every person."
- John Kekes: according to relativism, what people value depends on the context of their birth, genetic inheritance, experiences, and political, cultural, economic and religious influences - on subjective attitudes, not objective features of values. So there cannot be a uniquely reasonable system of values.
- Relativism suggests right and wrong vary with cultural and social conditions, so no universal agreement is possible.

WHERE DOES RELATIVISM COME FROM?
- 1. A certain understanding of conscience: if we always follow conscience, right and wrong depend on what each person believes. This is NOT the Christian understanding of conscience. Example: "I think that it is okay to take drugs, my conscience is clear, and that's the important thing."
- 2. The influence of circumstances: every situation is different, so there can be no universal code. Example: "In some circumstances it will be right for the poor to rob from the rich, so one can never say that it is wrong to steal."
- 3. The idea of tolerating all opinions: the desire to promote tolerance may lead to saying there is no objective moral theory. Examples: "If your culture allows people to marry at twelve years of age, then that is okay"; what is right for a polygamist Muslim differs from what is right for a married Christian, so laws should not discriminate against polygamy.
- These ways of thinking are very common and persuasive today.
- Phrase to discuss: relativism as "feet firmly planted in mid air".

DIFFICULTIES WITH RELATIVISM
- It would be very hard to set school rules or state laws, because good and bad would always depend on circumstances and personal belief.
- Extreme example - justifying terrorism: "I feel that it is right to kill others in order to achieve my political ends, so in my situation killing is right."

SUMMARY
- Pluralism makes agreement on the common good more challenging.
- Tolerance of other viewpoints is essential in debate, but there will always be conflict of opinion.
- Bioethics is the study of ethical issues in medicine.
- Conflict in debate often stems from differing underlying ethical viewpoints.
- Fundamentalism and relativism are extreme viewpoints found in modern debates.

KEY TERMS
- Pluralism: many different schools of thought in one society, each with a right to its cultural and religious practices.
- Tolerance: accepting others' right to hold and express a view we disagree with.
- Bioethics: the study of ethical issues in medicine.
- Fundamentalism: following a truth literally and the law strictly, without exception.
- Dogmatism: asserting beliefs (with literalism, a mark of fundamentalism).
- Literalism: taking the literal meaning of words or texts.
- Relativism: the view that there is no objective right or wrong; truth is subjective.
- Argumentum ad hominem: attacking the person instead of the argument.
- Subjective view: the belief of the individual. Objective view: a universal truth that applies everywhere.

rows.prompt: Outline the arguments for and against stem-cell research using human embryos, and identify the causes of conflict in this debate. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Stem cells are versatile cells that can reproduce themselves and make more specialised cells, so they may help treat Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, heart disease, stroke and diabetes. UK law allows research on foetal tissue up to fourteen days old. Supporters argue that experimentation has always been part of medical research, that it may bring great advances against diseases like cancer, and that no person is harmed. A polio vaccine was found using discarded foetuses, and spare IVF embryos will be discarded anyway, so with consent they should be used well. Their principle is the greater good of humanity; they see the embryo as a potential life and believe consequences can make an act right. Opponents argue the embryo is a human life and must never be used as a means to an end. Experimentation needs consent, which an embryo cannot give, and the Helsinki Declaration condemns research without consent. In doubt we should err on the side of caution. Their principle is that a person must not be used for experiments without consent; the end does not justify the means. The Catholic Church opposes the research because the embryo is a human life, and the Pontifical Academy for Life (2003) says embryos deserve 'the full respect that is due to every human person'. The two causes of conflict are how people view the status of the embryo and whether results can make an action morally right.

rows.prompt: Using one social ethics debate you have studied, outline the arguments on each side and identify the underlying ethical positions that cause the conflict. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: In recent Irish debates on sexuality in public life, one issue was whether the State should recognise the marriage of homosexual people. Those in favour argued that every person has a right to marry whatever their sexual orientation, and to deny that right is discrimination. Marriage would bring stability to gay relationships and make it easier to access civil rights, such as inheritance rights, and would make society more aware of the equality of gay people. Their moral principle is equality of opportunity for every person. Their underlying ethical position is that homosexuality is a reality in the nature of human persons and should be fully accepted. Those against argued that marriage is the bonding of a man and a woman, that same-sex marriage goes against the code of belief of many religions, and that refusing it is not discrimination but loyalty to marriage as a union of man and woman open to new life. Their moral principle is that marriage is of its essence a lifelong bond of a man and a woman supported by family and children. Their underlying position is that homosexual acts are against the moral law and natural law. The Catholic Church rejects such marriage; CCC 2360 says sexuality 'is ordered to the conjugal love of man and woman'. The causes of conflict are multilayered: supporters focus on respect for difference and human rights, while many opponents say their stance comes from their concept of marriage and family, not homophobia.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Arguments for (4-5 marks); moral principle and position for (2-3); arguments against (4-5); moral principle and position against (2-3); causes of conflict (3-4). Candidates may instead use the stem-cell debate if presented as social/bioethical; credit accurate use of the chapter's material.

rows.prompt: Explain the role of tolerance in a pluralist society, and describe two fallacies that should be avoided in moral debate. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: In a pluralist society there are many schools of thought, and all groups have a right to their cultural and religious practices. Tolerance is a frame of mind that accepts others' right to hold and express a view we disagree with, and it protects religious and civil liberties. But it is not the final answer: a society must live by some common values, and we cannot tolerate what is destructive, such as bullying. In debate, argumentum ad hominem should be avoided: it attacks the person, not the issue, e.g. 'you don't even dress yourself decently!' Emotive language should also be avoided: it plays on fears, prejudices and stereotypes, or uses one anecdote to generalise, as when all asylum-seekers are called 'spongers'.
rows.marking_scheme: Tolerance: definition 2 marks + role/limits 2 marks. Two fallacies x 3 marks (name 1 + explanation/example 2). Fallacies: argumentum ad hominem; emotions and loyalties colouring judgement; emotive language/stereotypes/anecdotes.
